[[File:Daniel Simon Mills.jpg|thumb|Professor D S Mills]]
'''Daniel Simon Mills''', [[Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons|FRCVS]] (born 21 August 1966) is an English [[veterinarian]] and [[biologist]] and the UK's first Professor of Veterinary Behavioural Medicine based at the [[University of Lincoln]], United Kingdom. He attended [[St Edmund's College, Ware]] before studying at the [[University of Bristol]] where he received his [[Bachelor of Veterinary Science|BVSc]] degree and completed his PhD degree in [[ethology|animal behaviour]] from [[De Montfort University]].

==Biography==

After some time spent in general practice, he became a Lecturer, Senior Lecturer and Principal Lecturer in animal behaviour at De Montfort University, and subsequently the [[University of Lincoln]], where he has been Head of the Department of Biological Sciences, and now heads up the clinical animal behaviour team. He has an active teaching and research portfolio.  His research has focused on the assessment of emotion in companion animals and the use of semiochemicals to manage their problem behaviour (pheromonatherapy<ref>{{Cite web|title=Pheromonatherapy|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/241844473|access-date=27 June 2021|website=ResearchGate publication archive}}</ref>). He has led the development of what has become known as the psychobiological approach to animal behaviour assessment,<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1 August 2017|title=Perspectives on assessing the emotional behavior of animals with behavior problems|url=http://eprints.lincoln.ac.uk/id/eprint/27040/1/27040%20COBEHA_361_edit_report.pdf|journal=Current Opinion in Behavioral Sciences|language=en|volume=16|pages=66–72|doi=10.1016/j.cobeha.2017.04.002|issn=2352-1546|last1=Mills |first1=Daniel S. |s2cid=53186534 }}</ref> and has published more than 200 full scientific papers, books and chapters.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Mills DS|url=https://scholar.google.co.uk/citations?user=lhReXNYAAAAJ&hl=en&oi=sra|access-date=2021-06-27|publisher=Google Scholar}}</ref>

Among his achievements are becoming the first person within the UK to be recognised as a specialist in veterinary behavioural medicine by the [[Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons]].<ref>[http://www.shootingstar-pr.co.uk/index.php?page=professor-daniel-mills-for-companian-animal-behaviour UK's first specialist in veterinary behavioural medicine] Accessed 15 November 2010</ref>  and being awarded Fellowship of the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons in 2016 in recognition of his contribution to the field. In 2020 he was also listed in the top 2% of scientists in the world<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ioannidis|first1=John P. A.|last2=Boyack|first2=Kevin W.|last3=Baas|first3=Jeroen|date=16 October 2020|title=Updated science-wide author databases of standardized citation indicators|journal=PLOS Biology|volume=18|issue=10|article-number=e3000918|doi=10.1371/journal.pbio.3000918|pmid=33064726 |issn=1545-7885|pmc=7567353 |doi-access=free }}</ref>  and in 2021 was in the top 1% of cited scientists.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Updated science-wide author databases of standardized citation indicators |url=https://elsevier.digitalcommonsdata.com/datasets/btchxktzyw/3 |website=Updated science-wide author databases of standardized citation indicators}}</ref> The psychobiological approach to animal behaviour assessment, which he has pioneered, provides a scientific framework for making inferences about motivational and emotional state in animals.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Animals and Us: 50 years and more of applied ethology |publisher=Wageningen Academic Publishers |year=2016 |isbn=978-90-8686-282-5 |location=Wageningen, the Netherlands |pages=966–981}}</ref>  His recognised practical achievements include the development of the Lincoln stable mirror to assist horses with isolation problems<ref>[http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk/1536918.stm Stable mirrors and horse welfare] Accessed 15 November 2010</ref> and validation of the use of animal pheromones<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.lincoln.ac.uk/news/2013/01/624.asp |title=News and Press &#124; University of Lincoln |website=lincoln.ac.uk |access-date=25 March 2013}}</ref> to influence unwanted behaviour; he has also developed a series of freely available, validated, psychometric instruments<ref>{{Cite web|title=canine behaviour calculators|url=https://ipstore.lincoln.ac.uk/product/online-canine-behaviour-calculators|url-status=live|access-date=27 June 2021|website=online behaviour calculators|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210627101157/https://ipstore.lincoln.ac.uk/product/online-canine-behaviour-calculators |archive-date=2021-06-27 }}</ref> for assessment of emotional predisposition in dogs. He has appeared on several scientific and popular television programmes, such as the  [[Horizon (BBC TV series)]] programme: the Secret Life of the Dog <ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b00pssgh/clips |title=BBC Two – Horizon, 2009–2010, the Secret Life of the Dog – Clips |publisher=BBC |access-date=25 March 2013}}</ref> and  [[Bang Goes the Theory]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b01hkyhp |title=BBC One – Bang Goes the Theory, Series 6, Episode 8 |publisher=BBC |access-date=25 March 2013}}</ref> Since 2020, he has run an occasional  podcast series "What makes you click?", in which he chats with colleagues from the field of clinical animal behaviour and welfare.

== Selected works ==
* ''The Domestic Horse: The Origins, Development and Management of its Behaviour'', with Sue. M. McDonnell (2005)
* ''BSAVA Manual of Canine and Feline Behavioural Medicine'', with Debra.F. Horwitz (2009)
* ''The Encyclopedia of Applied Animal Behaviour and Welfare'', with [[Jeremy Marchant Forde]], Paul McGreevy, David Morton, Christine Nicol, Clive Phillips, Peter Sandoe and Ronald Swaisgood (2010)
* ''Stress and Pheromonatherapy'' with Helen Zulch and Maya Dube (2013)
* ''Dog Bites: A Multidisciplinary Perspective'', with Carri Westgarth (2017)
